items.stem: What is meant by malware?
options: Malicious code that redirects a user from a genuine website to a fake one to capture personal data
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system
Software that secretly records user activity such as key presses and sends it to a third party
Software designed to damage a system or gain unauthorised access, e.g. viruses, worms, spyware, ransomware
items.answer: Software designed to damage a system or gain unauthorised access, e.g. viruses, worms, spyware, ransomware
items.markingKey: malware: software designed to damage a system or gain unauthorised access, e.g. viruses, worms, spyware, ransomware.

items.stem: Explain the difference between phishing and pharming.
items.answer: Phishing relies on the user clicking a link in a fake email; pharming uses malicious code/DNS poisoning to redirect the user to a fake website even when the correct address is typed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: phishing — email/link from apparently trusted source; 1 mark: pharming — redirection without user action [2]

items.stem: Explain how a virus differs from a worm.
items.answer: A virus attaches to a file/program and needs the user to run it to spread; a worm is standalone and replicates itself across networks automatically.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Customers of GreenLeaf Pharmacy report that the company website looks slightly different and asks for card details twice. Describe two signs that should make the user suspicious.
items.answer: Spelling errors; generic greeting; urgent request; unexpected attachment; URL not matching; no HTTPS padlock.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Customers of Pioneer Insurance report that the company website looks slightly different and asks for card details twice. (a) Describe two actions the organisation should take to reduce the risk. (b) Explain the possible consequences for the organisation.
items.answer: (a) Staff training; email filters; anti-malware; firewall; regular backups; 2FA. (b) Data stolen/lost; financial loss; reputational damage; legal penalties; downtime.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.stem: Coral Bay Aquarium in Mexico City stores the personal details of 50 000 customers. Discuss the threats to the data held by Coral Bay Aquarium and how serious each is.
items.answer: Points in favour: malware can corrupt or encrypt data; hacking can steal customer data; phishing and pharming target staff and customers to obtain passwords. Points against / limitations: the likelihood of each threat depends on staff awareness and existing defences; some threats are reduced by back-ups and training. Conclusion: phishing is often the most serious because it bypasses technical defences through people.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. items.stem: GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Accra has recently suffered a data breach. Evaluate the security measures GreenLeaf Pharmacy should use to protect its customer data.

items.stem: What is validation?
options: Encrypting data
Removing duplicate data
A check that data has been copied accurately
A check by the computer that data is reasonable and meets set rules
items.answer: A check by the computer that data is reasonable and meets set rules
items.markingKey: Validation cannot ensure data is correct, only sensible/allowed.

items.stem: Explain why validation cannot guarantee that data is correct.
items.answer: Validation only checks data is reasonable/within rules; a wrong value that is still within the rules (e.g. age 34 instead of 43) is accepted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: only checks rules; 1 mark: example of valid but wrong data [2]

items.stem: Describe how double entry is used as a verification method.
items.answer: The data is entered twice (e.g. a new password); the computer compares the two entries and asks for re-entry if they differ.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: The 7-bit data 1011001 is to be sent using odd parity, with the parity bit as the most significant bit. Give the 8-bit byte that is sent.

items.stem: Four bytes are received using even parity: 11010111, 01001000, 10010101, 01010100. Identify the byte that contains an error and explain how you know.
items.answer: Byte 4 (01010100): it has 3 ones, which is odd, but even parity is used.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: byte 4; 1 mark: counts 1s and compares with even parity [2]

items.stem: Four bytes are received using even parity: 00000110, 01001111, 01101100, 00101101. Identify the byte that contains an error and explain how you know.

(b) The data is entered twice (e.g. a new password); the computer compares the two entries and asks for re-entry if they differ.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: row and column parity; 1 mark: intersection identifies bit [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Staff at Horizon Travel type orders from paper forms into a new computer system and send them to a warehouse over a network. (a) Explain the difference between validation and verification in this context. (b) Describe how data is verified when it is sent to the warehouse. (c) Explain one limitation of parity checks.
items.answer: (a) Validation: the system checks entered data follows rules; verification: checks the data entered/transferred matches the original. (b) Parity checks / checksums calculated by sender and receiver; if mismatch, data re-sent (ARQ). (c) They cannot detect an even number of bit errors and cannot correct errors (unless a parity block is used).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3] (c) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: What is meant by a worm?
options: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system
Software that secretly records user activity such as key presses and sends it to a third party
Malicious code that redirects a user from a genuine website to a fake one to capture personal data
Malware that replicates itself across a network without needing to attach to a file
items.answer: Malware that replicates itself across a network without needing to attach to a file
items.markingKey: a worm: malware that replicates itself across a network without needing to attach to a file.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how a virus differs from a worm. (b) Explain the difference between phishing and pharming.
items.answer: (a) A virus attaches to a file/program and needs the user to run it to spread; a worm is standalone and replicates itself across networks automatically. (b) Phishing relies on the user clicking a link in a fake email; pharming uses malicious code/DNS poisoning to redirect the user to a fake website even when the correct address is typed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: phishing — email/link from apparently trusted source; 1 mark: pharming — redirection without user action [2]

items.stem: Northfield Academy in Dubai stores the personal details of 50 000 customers. Assess the threats to the data held by Northfield Academy and how serious each is.
items.answer: Points in favour: malware can corrupt or encrypt data; hacking can steal customer data; phishing and pharming target staff and customers to obtain passwords. Points against / limitations: the likelihood of each threat depends on staff awareness and existing defences; some threats are reduced by back-ups and training. Conclusion: phishing is often the most serious because it bypasses technical defences through people.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a strong password policy improves security. (b) Describe how a firewall protects a network.
items.answer: (a) Long passwords with mixed character types are harder to guess or crack by brute force; regular changes limit damage if one is stolen. (b) It sits between the network and the internet; examines incoming and outgoing packets against rules (addresses, ports, protocols); blocks unauthorised traffic and logs attempts.

items.stem: The managers of Sunrise Bakery have asked Mateo to review security. Discuss the security measures Sunrise Bakery should use to protect its customer data.
items.answer: Points in favour: user accounts and strong passwords with 2FA; access rights by role; firewall; encryption of stored and transmitted data; anti-malware; back-ups. Points against / limitations: measures cost money and staff time; strong rules may annoy users who then write passwords down; no measure is complete without staff training. Conclusion: a layered approach with training gives the best protection.
